title: Amazon's CEO Andy Jassy Just Announced Huge News for Amazon Investors
detail:
Amazon's CEO Andy Jassy Just Announced Huge News for Amazon Investors
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 1:20 PM MST 3 min read
AMZN
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Andy Jassy is the CEO of Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), succeeding founder Jeff Bezos a few years ago. Jassy used to lead Amazon Web Services (AWS), and his appointment as CEO a few years ago clearly indicated that this was the direction Amazon's business was heading. Bezos was correct in this assessment, as AWS has become a huge part of Amazon's business.

However, it's about to get even bigger. Andy Jassy made a bold prediction during Amazon's third-quarter earnings call that investors need to digest, as it could have big implications for the stock.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

CEO Andy Jassy Amazon: Image source: Amazon.com Inc.
AWS is headed to the $1 trillion mark

During Amazon's Q3 earnings call, Jassy noted that AWS could grow by more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, driven by significant investments in the platform. Over the next five to 10 years, that could grow to become a $1 trillion business. For reference, AWS, Amazon's cloud computing unit, grew at 39% in Q3, and its trailing-12-month sales totaled $161 billion.

That's huge news for investors, but what does it mean for the stock?

The biggest thing investors must realize is just how much better of a business AWS is than commerce. Commerce businesses in general operate on razor-thin margins, and while Amazon is one of the best at maximizing its margins, it's still much lower than what AWS puts up. During Q3, AWS' operating margin reached 39% on operating income of $17.8 billion. Its North American commerce segment delivered $8.7 billion in operating income on a 7.7% margin.

That's a huge mismatch, and it shows why Amazon is investing in AWS so heavily: It has a superior operating profile. As Amazon leans more heavily into AWS, it will be great news for the stock. Let's assume AWS hits a $1 trillion run rate a decade from now. If Amazon can maintain a 39% margin, that's $390 billion in operating income. Over the past 12 months, Amazon has produced $106 billion in operating income.

AMZN Operating Income (TTM) data by YCharts.

That means its operating income could more than quadruple over the next decade, which would result in huge returns for shareholders. AWS headed to $1 trillion in annual revenue would be huge news for investors, and if Jassy is right, could indicate that Amazon is a top stock to buy in the market now.

Markets are trembling amid the latest AI stock sell-off, which has sent shares of major AI players deep into the red. But CNBC's Jim Cramer believes the downturn is not another dot-com crash.

Cramer warned that AI stocks could fall further, particularly semiconductor companies whose shares surged during the AI boom. However, he argued that unlike the speculative businesses that collapsed in 2000, many of today's AI companies are highly profitable.

His biggest concern is smaller AI infrastructure companies such as CoreWeave, Iren and Nebius, which have borrowed heavily to finance data center projects that could face regulatory delays.

Before the election too, Cramer was more careful about tech. On Mad Money, he said the Nasdaq had just closed its worst month since March 2025 and that the week ahead "might be even worse." He said he wanted to see a "crescendo" before putting more money into tech, which he described as stocks getting crushed in the morning and then rallying on big volume to finish higher. He also warned that anti-data center politicians could stop projects if Democrats took control, and data center stocks fell on Wednesday on fears of tighter AI regulation, Reuters reported.

title: Qualcomm CEO: Its Data Center Ramp Is “All Supply Bound,” Not Demand Bound
detail:
Qualcomm CEO: Its Data Center Ramp Is “All Supply Bound,” Not Demand Bound
Roxanna Maglangit
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 12:25 PM MST 6 min read
QCOM
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Qualcomm CEO: Its Data Center Ramp Is "All Supply Bound," Not Demand Bound ©@MrWashingt0n from pixabay via Canva, @Evgenii Sudarev from Best4Best via Canva
Key Takeaways

Qualcomm stock fell about 11% this week after its earnings guidance for the December quarter came in below expectations.

CEO Cristiano Amon says supply is the only thing limiting the company's $5 billion data center revenue target for fiscal 2027.

Most of that $5 billion comes from two hyperscalers. One of them is Amazon, and Qualcomm puts the potential revenue from its AWS agreement at up to $60 billion over 10 years.

At 17x forward earnings, close to its three-year average while earnings fall, the stock prices in little of the data center ramp. Shrinking margins are the main risk.

Qualcomm (QCOM:NASDAQ) stock fell about 11% this week. Its earnings guidance for the December quarter disappointed, and rising chip costs overshadowed its non-handset growth.

But CEO Cristiano Amon wants investors looking at a different part of the business. On CNBC's Halftime Report on Thursday, he was asked about data centers:

"I tell you right now, regardless of all this noise, I think the $5 billion commitment we made, it's not demand bound, it's all supply bound. If I have more supply, I'll probably do better than $5 billion."

That's about as confident as a CEO gets on a down day.

On Wednesday's fourth-quarter call, CFO Akash Palkhiwala added a useful detail. Qualcomm is "very well positioned from a supply perspective to execute on the $5 billion target." Supply only limits growth above $5 billion.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Qualcomm, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Qualcomm's Analyst Ratings

Amazon is the anchor customer

Qualcomm guides data center revenue above $650 million in the December quarter. Palkhiwala expects the business to end fiscal 2027 at about a $7 billion annual run rate, and management's target for fiscal 2029 is more than $15 billion.

On the call, Amon said most of fiscal 2027's $5 billion comes from two hyperscalers, and one of them is Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ). Qualcomm's custom accelerators for Amazon Web Services started shipping in October, and its connectivity chips for AWS ramp later in November.

Palkhiwala also put the AWS agreement's potential revenue at up to $60 billion over the next 10 years. That's the deal Qualcomm signed in September. Spread evenly, it comes to $6 billion a year from Amazon alone, which is more than the whole fiscal 2027 target (assuming Amazon reaches the top of that range). Amazon also holds a warrant for up to 25 million Qualcomm shares, so it has a stake in this going well.

title: 4 Stocks I'm Not Selling Even If the Fed Keeps Raising Rates
detail:
4 Stocks I'm Not Selling Even If the Fed Keeps Raising Rates
Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 11:37 AM MST 6 min read
BRK-B
JNJ
AMZN
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September, and another hike is widely expected by the end of the year. The relationship between higher interest rates and stock market returns is complicated, but because higher rates raise the cost of borrowing, they can put downward pressure on equity markets as investors brace for lower corporate earnings.

This is certainly a meaningful risk worth monitoring, but there are plenty of stocks that could perform well over the long run regardless of whether the Fed raises interest rates again soon. Four of my holdings fit the bill, in my view, and I intend to keep all four intact well beyond the next interest rate increase. Here are these four stocks: Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT), and Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
1. Johnson & Johnson

Johnson & Johnson's business is relatively insensitive to interest rate hikes, a tool the Federal Reserve uses to slow spending and economic activity and rein in inflation. This can lead to lower demand for many products and services, but not for the kind that Johnson & Johnson offers. The pharmaceutical giant boasts a deep pipeline of lifesaving drugs, which should remain in high demand regardless of economic conditions. Johnson & Johnson's medical device business is also fairly resilient. And on top of that, Johnson & Johnson boasts a rock-solid balance sheet.

Perhaps the best evidence for that claim is the company's AAA rating -- the highest rating possible -- from S&P Global. Of course, none of that guarantees that Johnson & Johnson will perform well over the next year. But the company's business is well-equipped to navigate a high-interest rate environment and continue performing well long after, as it expands its product lineup through innovation. Finally, Johnson & Johnson is a fantastic income stock. It has increased its dividends for 64 consecutive years, making it a Dividend King, or a stock with at least 50 straight annual payout hikes.

2. Amazon

Amazon has a vast business that spans e-commerce, cloud computing, advertising, video and music streaming, and more. Some of the company's segments could experience lower demand if interest rates continue to rise. For instance, corporations may reduce their advertising budgets and demand fewer cloud services as customers cut retail spending. This may lead to lower revenue and earnings than the tech leader would otherwise generate. But I'd stick with Amazon through thick and thin. Here's why.
